assumptions: a parts catalog with per-model-year coverage, or an accepted plan to answer 'not covered' honestly for the vehicles you cannot price
a price source with enough freshness to quote at auction time, and a stated tolerance for how stale is too stale
labour-cost assumptions per region, since the repair estimate and therefore the Total Loss verdict depend on them even though the page never names them
a review path for the regulatory vocabulary: cite the standards and thresholds you invoke, or drop the claims that read like compliance approval
clone_cost.estimate: 5-7 weeks for a single-jurisdiction version a buyer would trust; a year of data work for the catalog that makes it worth using
clone_cost.why: The application is ordinary: photo preprocessing with Sharp, a queue on Inngest, Prisma over Postgres, Next.js and Stripe, and a multimodal model call with search grounding for part numbers and live prices - two or three weeks for someone fluent in that stack. The time goes into the parts catalog and the pricing source, which are the only defensible parts of the product and are not built here at all: structuring OEM data per make, model and year, keeping prices from becoming stale, and deciding what to return when coverage is thin. Adding a second jurisdiction (ECE instead of DOT/SAE, EUR, per-country import and inspection rules) is a further multiplier rather than a config flag. A clone can reproduce the flow quickly; it cannot reproduce the asset.

hazard_note: This is a money decision dressed in regulatory vocabulary. The product returns a Total Loss verdict and a repair estimate that a buyer may bid against, while invoking DOT, SAE and ECE standards, country-specific import, title, emissions and inspection requirements, and a Loss Ratio band policy described as 'matching EU & US salvage threshold standards' with no citation and no named issuing body for either threshold. Nothing on the page states who is liable when the estimate is wrong, no accuracy figure exists for either the part identification or the price, and the resale denominator comes from another estimate rather than a transaction record, so a High-band verdict near a boundary can flip on inputs that are both soft. The team's stated posture is the right instinct - a wrong OEM code shown with false confidence is worse than no result - but an interface banner is not a compliance sign-off, and a tool that names regulators should either cite them or stop invoking them. Held from promotion on that basis: publishable as a documented case, not as a usable figure.

prior_art.relation: both turn a stream of sensor evidence into a regulatory-flavoured verdict for a human to act on, and neither page publishes an accuracy figure - the fisheries tool goes further and states there is no ground truth for its risk classification, while Carbender's page implies its bands come from external standards without naming them. Read together, they are the two failure modes of the same design: admit the measurement problem, or borrow authority from a regulator.

both end in an artifact a person checks rather than an action the system takes - a repair plan PDF against a cited diff - and both leave the accuracy of the underlying judgement unmeasured. The difference is what they attach evidence to: Continuity grounds a claim against the live web and shows the citation next to the verdict, while Carbender grounds a part number against a proprietary catalog the reader cannot inspect, so its traceability stops at the vendor boundary.

both put a machine-readable judgement in front of a purchase decision and both monetise through the transaction surface rather than the model; the marketplace tool's advantage is that its output is checked by the market on the next listing, whereas a repair estimate is only checked when the parts arrive, so the feedback loop is months long.

what_breaks_first: Catalog coverage, on both ends of the pipeline. The 700,000-row figure is spread over 60-plus makes and their model years, so the first user with a twelve-year-old European hatchback gets either no parts or a plausible wrong code - and the scarcity banner only helps if scarcity is detected against coverage the product actually measures rather than against a lookup that happens to miss. Second, the severity-to-cost link: the bands assume the repair estimate is close enough to divide by resale value, and near 40 and 70 percent a modest error in labour or parts changes 'repairable' into 'Total Loss' with no stated error model to tell the buyer which side of the line they are on. Third, spatial normalisation: the driver-side versus passenger-side disambiguation is the difference between quoting a mirror or a fender, and a cropped, low-light auction photo is precisely where a 3D-normalisation step degrades.
what_to_steal: Publish the decision rule, not just the score: the Loss Ratio names both inputs, states the band edges, and returns a verdict - a reader can recompute it and argue with it, which is more than most 'AI estimate' products offer. Then steal the failure-surface design: scarcity detection wired to an advisory banner, with the explicit principle that admitting no coverage beats a confident wrong answer. Region should be an input, not a translation - standards family, currency and title/import/emissions/inspection rules change what the estimate means, so carry them through the model call and the UI together. Free adjacent utility as acquisition: a VIN-to-window-sticker generator that costs nothing to run and lands the same audience on the paid product. And three model tiers with automatic failover in a flow running against an auction clock.
worth_note: The audience is specific and it pays: people bidding on salvage lots, body shops and mechanics, for whom a photo-to-parts-list-with-prices replaces a guess made in a ten-minute walk-around. Within that audience the wedge is real and better than the obvious alternative, because the two things a human estimator cannot do at an auction - check a 700,000-row OEM catalog and price parts across a jurisdiction boundary - are exactly what the build automates, and the Loss Ratio turns a pile of numbers into the one decision the buyer came with. What keeps it niche rather than strong is that the mechanism does not outlive the project: vision plus grounded pricing plus a published decision ratio is a well-executed instance of a pattern that will be repeated, and the moat is the catalog, not the method. No accuracy figure anywhere means a buyer inherits the author's confidence rather than a measured one - which the page at least admits is the wrong thing to hand over, hence the scarcity banners.
